Losing the third quarter by two, the Silver Ferns, as in the first game, went on to win the last quarter, with centre Kimiora Poi, captain Karin Burger and young defender Laura Blamer adding valuable punch in the second half.
Continuing to explore their playing combinations, the Silver Ferns reshuffled their starting seven for the second match.

The finishing shooting duo of game one, Grace Nweke and Martina Salmon, got the start with Maddy Gordon retaining the wing attack bib and teaming up with centre Tayla Earle in the midcourt. Silver Ferns coach Dame Noeline Taurua went with the young duo of Parris Mason at wing defence and Carys Stythe at goal defence, bookended by veteran Kelly Jackson.
Ball retention was a key work-on but sustaining the accuracy and consistency proved a tough ask as the Net Blacks impressed with their slick play and speed of movement.
The Net Blacks shooting duo of Mikaira Raerino and Thomson Matuku were difficult to stop.

Nweke was accurate on the shot but the constant pressure of Net Blacks defenders meant she didn't get enough ball in hand. At the other end, the one-handed lay-ups of Raerino were almost unstoppable as the Net Blacks kicked out to a 19-13 first quarter lead.
Peta Toeava replaced Gordon for the second quarter after she was sent for a concussion test following a heavy fall.
Attacking opportunities dried up for the Silver Ferns as the Net Blacks powered to a 38-21 lead at the main break.

The Silver Ferns made multiple changes for the second half, including the introduction of shooter Aliyah Dunn, the only player of the 14 not to play a part in game one. It was the 27-year-olds first return to the black dress since 2018.
A more concerted effort on attack saw more ball getting into the hands of shooters Te Paea Selby-Rickit and Dunn as the Silver Ferns competed on level terms through an evenly contested third spell.
The Silver Ferns close out a busy 2026 schedule with the final match against the New Zealand men's team in Hamilton on Saturday.

That's the message from Māori artist and rugby league supporter Charles Williams, who told RNZ the celebrations surrounding the Rugby League World Cup are about something much bigger than what happens on the field.
Despite the Kiwis suffering a big loss to the Kangaroos in the final, across Tāmaki Makaurau and beyond, supporters took to the streets waving flags, singing and celebrating their whakapapa.

At the centre of many of those celebrations was Williams (Ngāti Kahungunu ki te Wairoa, Te Whakatohea, Tūhoe, Ngāpuhi), who organised a series of parades to bring people together in support of the Kiwis.
The idea was inspired by the passion of Tongan supporters during the 2017 Rugby League World Cup.

"2017, the Tongan fans really took fandom to another level. So they went all out and they were basically riding solo. During that 2017 campaign, we saw them all over the streets of South Auckland, where I live.
"Post World Cup, I went to Tonga, did an art project over there, got to meet them and got to see even more the fan base there and how crazy they are.
"Come 2026, I really wanted us to kind of just get off the couch, really get out of the house. Let's be inspired by our whānau from Tonga, Samoa."
Williams approached New Zealand Rugby League with the idea and rallied friends to help bring the parades to life.
It began with around 50 people gathering at Māngere Bridge during the first week of the tournament. By the second week, the crowds had grown to hundreds, and the flags kept coming.

"I've noticed in this World Cup, there's been more of an emphasis on, yeah, hey, I'm from Tonga, Samoa, Cook Islands, Fiji, Papua New Guinea, so on and so forth. And even guys who are not a part of the Rugby League World Cup are jumping in.

"Guys from Niue, all of a sudden you got yellow flags all over the streets. They want to be proud of themselves and everyone wants to be proud of themselves. They want to stand up and go, 'Hey, here I am, here we are and we're from here.'
"And that's awesome, you know, and I love it. And I want people to really be proud of where they're from."
But the parades also prompted a bigger reflection for Williams about how Māori come together as a people, and how those gatherings are perceived by others.
Māori flags, including the Tino Rangatiratanga flag and He Whakaputanga flag, are often seen at hīkoi and protests, where communities gather to advocate for their rights, identity and rangatiratanga.
Williams said some people mocked the parades online, questioning whether supporters were protesting or taking part in a hīkoi.
And while he understands why people might make that association, he said the celebrations offered a different opportunity to come together under the same flag.
"One thing I've been thinking about for a little bit is how do we celebrate as a people? So we're kind of like known as the 'fighting people'.

"A lot of the comments mocking us were, oh, are you guys protesting? You know what I mean? And it's like, cool. "You know, I understand why you say that, because literally, we are always protesting. But it's been the first time, not the first time ever, but it's like the first time I've seen thousands of people with a Tino Rangatiratanga flag, happy, celebrating, and we're not actually fighting for anything.
"We're not trying to like get anything. It's just like, bro, we're just happy."
"We're under this flag. We're under this banner. And to celebrate, it's just been like, finally, we're just like, we're just happy."

US singer Ella Langley has swept the Country Music Association Awards (CMAs), following the huge success of her breakthrough hit Choosin' Texas.

"At this point, I'm sick of me," the 27-year-old joked in her acceptance speech, having spent so much of the ceremony on stage. "I could quit tomorrow and have the best career of my life."
Choosin' Texas was also named single of the year and song of the year, leading Langley to joke in an acceptance speech: "This song is the gift that keeps on giving."
Ella Langley, who won six awards on the night, performed her song Loving Life Again
Langley won six awards in total, including female vocalist of the year, music video of the year and album of the year for Dandelion.
She also performed her song Loving Life Again with a string quartet, and duetted with Miranda Lambert for a performance of Snakeskin Boots.
Choosin' Texas made history in September after spending 23 weeks at the top spot on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. It has now spent 28 weeks in total at the summit.
Following her win, Langley took to social media and said: "Hard to put this night into words and what it means.
"Thank you to my fans. Thank you for loving this record, thank you for coming to my shows, thank you for believing in my artistry.
"This year has been the most incredible journey, and I want to thank you for sharing in that with me. I love y'all."
Langley also performed Snakeskin Boots with Miranda Lambert during the ceremony
Taylor Swift also performed at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years.
Her performance began with Swift walking backstage and featured cameo appearances from country stars including Brad Paisley, Little Big Town, Sugarland, and Brooks & Dunn.
Swift then sang her recent hit I Knew It, I Knew You, from the Toy Story 5 soundtrack, using a blue guitar with bedazzled clouds on it, in a nod to the animated franchise.
The singer also mixed in some of her 2006 country hit Our Song, while Keith Urban joined her on the banjo.
Taylor Swift used a Toy Story-themed guitar and performed alongside Keith Urban
She also presented a lifetime achievement award to country music duo Brooks & Dunn
Swift's performance came after she was inducted into both the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Songwriters Hall of Fame earlier this year.
Other winners on the night included Chris Stapleton who won male vocalist of the year, The Red Clay Strays who won vocal group of the year, and Brooks & Dunn with vocal duo of the year.
Meanwhile Stephen Wilson Jr won the new artist of the year award while Charlie Worsham won musician of the year.
The award ceremony began with a tribute to country music legend Dolly Parton, who died in August aged 80.
Ceremony host Lainey Wilson began the tribute by duetting with singer-songwriter Vince Gill on a rendition of Parton's I Will Always Love You.

Vince Gill and Lainey Wilson performed I Will Always Love You in tribute to Parton
Presenters at the ceremony included actor Glen Powell and Shaboozey
Kix Brooks and Ronnie Dunn, known as Brooks & Dunn, accepted the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award
There was also a firey performance of Who Told You That during the ceremony from Tucker Wetmore
Megan Moroney delivered a floral performance of Beautiful Things

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmge: Florence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery.
The actress wrote on Instagram , external how "stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend".
"I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"
She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."
In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."
Pugh has spoken out before about judgement about how women look
Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds".

"The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg.
"Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."
The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming".
"I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."
She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again".
"I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."

Professor Heather Widdows from Everyday Lookism , external , which campaigns to end body shaming, told BBC News: "Pugh is right that we are in a place where 'beauty standards are changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with'.
"A global beauty ideal makes impossible demands and normalises what were once extreme," added Widdows, who is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Warwick.

"We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people's bodies... in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people."

Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.
In 2024, she told the Times , external she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived".
"Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."
She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance.
"I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said.
"But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."

Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.

Pugh also said she had sued several publications earlier this year, claiming they published AI-generated images appearing to show her receiving cosmetic injections that were presented as real photographs.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq14: Fiona Harvey appeared on Piers Morgan Uncensored in 2024, after the release of Netflix's Baby Reindeer
A woman who allegedly inspired the stalker character Martha in the hit Netflix drama Baby Reindeer is to appear at Harrow Crown Court on charges of racially aggravated harassment without violence.
Fiona Harvey, 61, is accused of sending several emails and three voicemails including antisemitic material to lawyer Mark Lewis, between 4 September and 9 October 2025.
During a hearing at Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court on Thursday, the court heard that Lewis initially believed Harvey was a potential client.
Harvey of Camden, north London, did not indicate a plea, but elected for a Crown Court trial.
The charge is an either-way offence, which means it can be heard in either a magistrates' court or Crown Court.
She will next appear at Harrow Crown Court for a pre-trial preparation hearing on 17 December.
Harvey has previously identified herself as the woman on whom Martha is based, after the release of Richard Gadd's Emmy Award-winning series in 2024.
She is suing the streamer £128m for defamation, negligence and privacy violations, arguing that that Netflix told "brutal lies" about her to over 50 million viewers around the world.
Netflix denies the claim, which will be heard in front of a jury on May 18, 2027, at the US District Court for the Central District of California.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck20: Brydon stars in a new series Bill's Included as well-intentioned but overly enthusiastic divorcé Bill Beam
Rob Brydon has revealed he pretended to be his own agent at the start of his career when he was working as a TV and radio presenter in Wales.

The actor, best known for playing Stacey's Uncle Bryn in the hit sitcom Gavin and Stacey, told BBC One's Graham Norton Show , external he used to step into the role of his fake agent to arrange bookings for events.
"I would get asked to go and do things, and I didn't really have an agent at that time so I invented a guy called Richard Knight," Brydon told the show.
The fictional agent would phone organisers and negotiate a fee for Brydon's appearance, he said.
The actor, who grew up in Baglan, Port Talbot, shared an anecdote about being invited to a fundraiser and managing to get a fee for it.
"I'm terribly embarrassed," he told the show's host and fellow guests Cynthia Erivo, David Tennant and Laura Linney.

Brydon, known for his ability to mimic a range of celebrities, went on to impersonate the fictional Richard Knight asking for money in return for an appearance, with the agent describing Brydon as "an angel".
"I would go to these events and they would say 'oh I spoke to Mr Knight, he's quite a character', and I would say 'more than you realise'," Brydon told the show.

The 61-year-old actor stars in new sitcom Bill's Included in which he plays Bill Beam, a divorced man who rents his spare rooms to four students to stay financially afloat while "trying his very best to be their friend".
He told the Press Association he was drawn to his latest comedy role because he had missed acting in sitcoms since featuring in Gavin and Stacey.
The popular show ended in January 2010, although Christmas specials aired in 2019 and 2024.
While Brydon has since hosted shows including Destination X and Would I Lie To You?, the new show marks his return to the sitcom format.
"He calls himself a land-friend, not a landlord," Brydon said of his character Bill Beam.
Bill's Included will follow Bill and his lodgers as they muddle through "chaos, growing pains and unexpected friendships"
Dylan Brady, Ada Player, Harry Baxendale and Yasmin Al-Khudhairi join the cast as Bill's student lodgers Christian, Hettie, James and Zahra.
Brydon praised the young actors, saying he "loved being around them, partly because of their energy".
He said he also enjoyed hearing their perspective on the industry.
"They knew who was being cast in what, who was directing which projects and it reminded me of how I used to be," he said.
The actor also remarked on the "odd" feeling of being told by some of the actors that they grew up watching him on television.
He said: "I remember that at the end of filming, one of them said to me, 'Thanks for being nice and for spending time with us between set-ups'.
"My reaction was, 'Well, of course I did. We're all actors on this show.'"
Bill's Included will be available on BBC iPlayer and BBC One from 20 November.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmgr: Social media companies should "show some decency and take these videos down", the prime minister has said, following a government attempt to have a YouTube video featuring a message from the jailed comedian removed.
The site's owner Google refused a government request to remove the clip posted by Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.
Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
Speaking following a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin, Andy Burnham said it was "time that we focus on the victims and think about them," rather than "hearing from a convicted criminal".
He said: "I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. Why are we having to hear from him. We shouldn't be and certainly [victims] shouldn't be hearing from him."

But when pressed by the reporter if he wanted to change the law to take action, he replied: "I wouldn't leap to that. I would first say to the social media companies show some responsibility here, think of the victims - that's the main thing.
Google told BBC News it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".
It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."

On Sunday, Laura Brand shared a video on their Sunday Service channel on the website and read out a message from her husband in which he said: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."
The Prison Service of England and Wales asked for the video to be removed, on the basis it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.
A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".
Russell Brand prison message 'appalling' and being investigated, No 10 says
Minister criticises media for 'amplifying' Russell Brand's prison message
Met Police investigating more 'potential criminal allegations' about Brand
The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.

The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.

The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken, but housing minister Matthew Pennycook - who described the video as "abhorrent" - told BBC Breakfast that the government remained in "close dialogue" with the company.

Jess Phillips, the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the government "doesn't have the power to enforce that this video is taken down".

"It relies on YouTube, in this instance... to do the right thing, which is a much, much broader argument about whether Ofcom codes that are in the Online Safety Act are there actually to protect women," she said.

An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement that the current guidance was ultimately voluntary, and "any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament".

Phillips, describing Brand as an "absolute narcissist", suggested it was "very likely" the government would look at introducing a second online safety act to address gaps in the current regulatory framework.
"Before, we haven't had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings," she said. "This is an entirely new era."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6eq: The band have become known for their energetic live performances and interwoven four-part harmonies
Westside Cowboy have been announced as BBC Introducing Artist of the Year 2026.
Jimmy Bradbury, Reuben Haycocks, Aoife Anson O'Connell and Paddy Murphy formed the band in Manchester in 2023 and have since rocketed from the pub circuit to some of the UK's biggest festivals.

The award is presented to an up-and-coming artist or band who has, with the support of BBC Introducing, made a significant impact and has previously been won by Olivia Dean, Myles Smith and Tom Grennan.
Murphy, from Longridge in Lancashire, said the win put them in "good company", with Bradbury, from Shropshire, adding that it was "very flattering".

BBC Introducing supports new musical talent across the UK , providing a platform to propel new artists on to the local and national stage through 30 Introducing shows, three national radio shows and six shows across BBC Radio 1, Radio 1Xtra, Radio 2, 6Music, Radio 3 and Asian Network.
About 72,000 tracks from emerging UK artists supported by BBC Introducing make it on to the airwaves each year.

Westside Cowboy uploaded their debut single I've Never Met Anyone I Thought I Could Really Love (Until I Met You) to the Introducing platform in November 2024 and had their first play on radio within hours.
Murphy and Bradbury were surprised with the award during a radio interview
The four-piece played in various other bands before coming together to form Westside Cowboy.
Haycocks, O'Connell, and Murphy had met at Manchester's Royal Northern College of Music in 2021 and later got to know Bradbury after meeting him in the nearby Johnny Roadhouse music shop.

Murphy and Bradbury played in surf-rock trio Katz, while Murphy and Haycocks both worked together in noise-pop trio, DieKaiDie, but it was when Bradbury, who was working in the music shop repairing guitars, asked the others if they wanted to start a new band that Westside Cowboy's journey began.

By the time their second single, Shells, was released in April 2025, they had been been selected to play the BBC Introducing stage at Glastonbury Festival, and the song was put on the BBC 6Music playlist.

Their meteoric rise saw seen them appear on BBC music show Later... with Jools Holland in June and their debut album It Goes On was released on Island Records in August, peaking at number five in the UK charts.
Westside Cowboy reminisced about the early days on BBC Radio Manchester
Thanking the Introducing network and listeners for their support, Murphy said it was "really cool to be recognised for the music you make".
"We say this a lot, so apologies if we sound like a broken record, [but] it's funny with this band because... we started it with so little pretence or plan," he said.
"So whenever people give us something cool like [this award], it's all a bit surreal because it still feels like a weekend project that we now just get to do way more regularly.
Westside Cowboy formed in 2023, having played together in other bands
William Wolstenholme, presenter and producer of BBC Introducing in Lancashire & Cumbria, gave the band their first play and said he remembers messaging them to upload the track.
"Over the past two years, Westside Cowboy have become surely the most exciting band in Manchester, and therefore the country," he said.
"They've fast-tracked from the sweaty pubs of the city's student music scene to many of the most famous venues in the country.
"It's a rise whose speed can scarcely be believed, and one that has shocked much of the music industry."
He said the band's obvious camaraderie was one of their main selling points.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crwy: Harry Styles will compete with Cher for the weekend's most flamboyant outfit
Harry Styles will make his Glastonbury festival debut next year as one of the event's headliners, alongside Sam Fender and Billie Eilish - with Cher among the other stars on the bill.
The veteran US pop icon will play the coveted Sunday afternoon "legends" slot, which is often considered a fourth headline set. It will be her only UK festival appearance of the year.
Other acts on the line-up include Sombr, Sienna Spiro, Lily Allen, The Streets, Chase & Status, Kacey Musgraves, Primal Scream and breakout pop star Adéla.
Tickets for the festival sold out in just 42 minutes last month , with demand particularly high after the event took a year off in 2026.
Cher is bound to draw a huge crowd to hear hits like Turn Back Time, Believe and I Got You Babe
Electro pioneers Kraftwerk will make their Glastonbury debut with a headline set at West Holts - the festival's third-largest stage.

The event will also welcome experimental Canadian band Angine de Poitrine, who have drawn attention for their prog-rock sound and polka-dotted stage costumes; rap legends De La Soul and Mike D; and pop provocateur FKA Twigs.

"We are so happy to be coming back after our fallow year and, as we head into winter after that peaceful period, we wanted to give you an early musical taster of what's to come at Glastonbury 2027 with this spread of incredible artists," said organiser Emily Eavis.
"We can't wait to see you down here on Worthy Farm in June for some much-needed good times!"
The gates will open at Worthy Farm in Somerset to 200,000 fans on Wednesday 23 June, with music on the main stages kicking off on Friday 25 June.
Tickets prices are at an all-time high of £408, including a £5 booking fee per ticket.
Festival organiser Emily Eavis watched Sam Fender's set from the side of the stage in 2022
Sam Fender will headline the first night, in what will be his second appearance at the festival.
He last played in 2022, immediately before Billie Eilish, and fought back tears as thousands of fans chanted along to hits like Seventeen Going Under and Hypersonic Missiles.
"Me and the boys have never been here before," he said. "We've never been here as punters, never played here before and we're doing that all in one day, which is the most crazy experience."

He will return as one of the UK's biggest rock stars, having won the Mercury Prize for his third album, People Watching, in 2025. Earlier this year, his duet with Olivia Dean - Rein Me In - became the UK's longest-running number one single of all time.
Fender is expected to release a new album ahead of his Glastonbury slot, which will land in the middle of his catchily-titled Proper Massive Stadium Tour.
Billie Eilish was the youngest solo act to headline Glastonbury when she topped the bill in 2022
Harry Styles will take the Pyramid Stage crown on the Saturday.
It comes amid acclaim for his euphoric and athletic Together Together tour, which largely focuses on the understated dance anthems of his fourth album Kiss All The Time. Disco Occasionally.
The pop star has previously been spotted partying at the festival's late-night dance arenas, despite attempting to go incognito in tracksuits and sunglasses.
In 2022, he was rumoured to be making a guest appearance during Eilish's set after his music was played during an early-morning soundcheck - but the duet never materialised.
Instead, Eilish gave a universally well-received performance, described as "imperious [and] hugely engaging" by the Guardian, , external and "proof that the future is here" by the NME , external .
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjy5: Osian Morgan has previously appeared in Pobol y Cwm and Waterloo Road
Voicing Luke Skywalker in the Welsh-language version of Star Wars was a "dream job" according to actor Osian Morgan.
The Cardiff-born actor said he loved the film series as a child and playing one of the lead roles was "very exciting".
Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd - based on the original 1977 film Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope - was given its first showing at a red-carpet event in Cardiff on Thursday.
The dubbed Welsh version, featuring actors Matthew Rhys and Rhys Ifans, will be broadcast publicly for the first time by S4C on Christmas Day.
Almost half a century since A New Hope was first released, the sci-fi universe created by George Lucas remains one of the biggest film franchises of all time.
It has been translated into over 50 languages, with Welsh becoming its most recent.
"It feels very exciting, it's thrilling," said Morgan, who has previously starred in Welsh language soap opera Pobol y Cwm and in BBC drama Waterloo Road.
His family attended the first screening of Star Wars: Gobaith Newydd, and Morgan admitted his youngest brother had never seen any of the films before.
"Shout out to him because the first time he gets to see it in Welsh is great," he said.
The film's premiere in Cardiff included a rousing version of the theme tune

Mark Lewis Jones, who voices the dark lord Darth Vader, said on the red carpet it was "nice to record the voice but not have the make-up" and joked that "the Rhosllanerchrugog accent lends itself to the dark side".
Llyr Ifans, who plays C-3PO, said he hoped the film was successful and that more Welsh-language versions would follow.
"I'm quite confident it will go down well and there will be a lot of happy Welsh-speaking parents on Christmas Day."
Ifans said he been a fan of the Star Wars films since childhood, and getting invited to play the character was "surreal".
"When I first got the email through I thought 'wow, this is a bit weird doing Star Wars in Welsh' but playing C-3PO, one of the iconic parts, you can't say no, can you really?"
C-3PO is said to be fluent in six million forms of communication and Ifans said it was now one more.
Mark Lewis Jones, who voices Darth Vader, joked his accent 'lent itself to the dark side'
Prominent actors have lent their voices to the film's most famous characters, including Matthew Rhys (Han Solo), Rhys Ifans (Obi-Wan Kenobi) and Aimee-Ffion Edwards (Princess Leia).
Other voice actors in the Welsh version include Nia Roberts, Ioan Hefin, Richard Harrington, Owain Arthur, Rhodri Meilir, Richard Elfyn and Steffan Donnelly. The film is directed by Ellyn Stern.
The Welsh language version was announced at the National Eisteddfod in Pembrokeshire in August
The Welsh-language version was announced at the National Eisteddfod in Pembrokeshire in August, with Lucasfilm co-president Lynwen Brennan saying the franchise was keen to expand its horizons.
"As someone who was born and raised in Wales, seeing the audience reaction to iconic Star Wars moments retold in the Welsh language was a moment of great pride," she said.
S4C chief executive Geraint Evans added that working with "one of the most iconic and influential film franchises of all time is a tremendous honour".
"It is a unique opportunity to introduce the Welsh language to new audiences around the world, while showcasing Wales and its exceptional creative talent on a global stage," he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqj3: Page spoke of the inappropriate comments during Tuesday's episode of the reality show I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out Of Here!
Joanna Page has said she was subjected to "really inappropriate" and "awful" comments from a fellow actor while on set.
The Swansea-born actress, 48, told campmates on ITV's I'm a Celebrity… Get Me Out of Here! that the unnamed male actor had whispered "awful stuff" in her ear before a scene.
"He just spent the whole time just sort of making up this song and chanting about what he was going to do to me, and nobody said anything," she told fellow campmate Mariella Frostrup.
Page has previously described feeling forced to laugh off being groped while filming with a "handsy" TV presenter.

Page spoke of the inappropriate comments during Tuesday's episode of the reality show, as fellow celebrities, broadcaster Frostrup and model Leomie Anderson, discussed navigating male-dominated work environments in their careers.
Page said the actor had come up to her "before you were going to do a take or something".
Joanna Page is taking part in the 26th series of I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here
Frostrup suggested that if she did speak up people would say she could not "take it", and would call it "banter".
Page then asked her campmates if they thought "we've changed".
"I think it has changed," Frostrup said, "because I look at my daughter now, and she just wouldn't put up with anything like that."

Page, who started out as an actress in 1999, previously revealed in an autobiography that she was warned about a TV presenter being "very handsy" and was groped but stayed silent because she did not want to "make a fuss".
She said she tried to keep it "light-hearted" and "would not have dreamed of making a complaint".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6x2: Singer Julio Iglesias is facing an investigation by Spain's national court over allegations he sexually abused and assaulted two female former staff members
Two women, who worked for the 83-year-old in the Caribbean, have accused him of abuse which they say took place in the Bahamas and the Dominican Republic in 2021.
The announcement comes after Spanish prosecutors dropped an inquiry into the claims earlier this year after concluding that they lacked jurisdiction because the alleged crimes took place abroad.
Iglesias, who has been a household name in Spain since the 1960s and has sold millions of records worldwide, has previously denied the allegations .

But in a statement published on Wednesday , external (in Spanish), national court Judge Antonio Piña said the account given in the complaint, alongside preliminary evidence provided, justified opening criminal proceedings.
He added that the investigation would cover parts of the complaint relating to potential crimes against sexual freedom, as well as assault and degrading treatment.

But the court will not investigate claims made in the lawsuit of human trafficking or crimes against workers' rights. Piña said these allegations were dismissed after he looked into the hiring of the women and found there was "no deception or artifice involved".
Piña said the former employees had been summoned to testify in person on 3 February.
The announcement comes after Spain's public prosecutor's office shifted its position last month, saying it now believed the court had jurisdiction to investigate the allegations.
In its statement, the national court said Spanish law sets out that courts can hear cases of crimes committed abroad by Spanish citizens provided certain conditions are met.
The allegations against Iglesias first emerged in a joint three-year investigation between Spanish newspaper El Diario , external and television network Univision news, published in January.
In that investigation, the two women were identified as a domestic worker and a physical therapist, who described alleged sexual abuse and degrading working conditions.
The domestic worker, whose name was changed to Rebeca in the reports, said Iglesias would regularly call her to his room at the end of the day and would touch her inappropriately without consent.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4g: Freja, who "didn't expect to be chosen" as the winner, beat more than 1,000 entries from across the UK

Freja, from Cardiff, beat more than 1,000 entries from across the UK and said she was "so grateful" to be chosen.
Her design will be the official BBFC black card, which displays the age rating and classification details of the film before every cinema showing.
Freja's winning design will be shown as the official BBFC black card before every UK cinema screening
The Year nine student, whose favourite subject is art, only started oil painting three years ago.
Her mum Marie recalled the moment Freja found out about the competition while scrolling on social media.
"She just squealed and said, 'there's this competition where you can create a piece of art' and she loves making art. So, she was like, 'I'm gonna do it'."

Freja and her mum attended a fan screening event for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on The Reaping in London

Actor Ralph Fiennes said: "It looks wonderful, it's really amazing, I love it."
Freja only started oil painting three years ago, but her mum says she has always been a creative person

Speaking of her inspiration, Freja said: "I was inspired by this specific part in the trailer because it shows the Hunger Games arena to be a beautiful place and not the killing machine that it actually is."
Marie, who is a photographer, said her daughter has always been a creative person and "makes stuff all the time", filling their home with her creations.
Marie said her daughter spent more than a month on the piece and worked until the day of the deadline after she "locked in for a whole weekend" to get it done.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y: Watch: Jeff Bezos on involvement in casting Robert Pattinson as James Bond

'Good Bond vibes' - Hollywood locals react to Robert Pattinson cast as new 007
"There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.
Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.
In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."
The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.
The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.
Robert Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday
Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.
But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.
"We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said.
There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said.

"By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately un-debated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob."
The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas.
Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqrm: Experts are calling it the biggest breakthrough in pancreatic cancer treatment for decades - a daily pill that appears to shrink and possibly even eliminate tumours in some patients with one of the deadliest and hardest-to-treat cancers.
Cancer became undetectable on scans in one in 12 of the patients given daraxonrasib along with chemotherapy in early medical trials.
Tumours stopped growing in almost all of the 61 participants who had recently been diagnosed with advanced pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body.
But doctors stress it is a long way from knowing how long it might keep the disease at bay and should not be seen as a cure.
Cancer Research UK called it "the biggest leap forward in decades" for pancreatic cancer patients.
The charity's Dr Sam Godfrey told BBC News that the results were incredibly exciting. "What this new drug has done is it's found a way of drugging the undruggable.
"We are finally seeing progress in pancreatic cancer which is so long overdue."
Pancreatic cancer is notoriously hard to treat and has the lowest survival rate of all common cancers in the UK.
Although chemotherapy can shrink tumours a bit, the cancer often grows again.
Most patients with advanced disease survive months, not years.
Doctors hope the new treatment might offer patients more time, even if it cannot stop cancers for good.
The trial followed patients for a year and a half, on average, and some did not see their cancer return during this time.
Longer studies are needed to understand if any of these cancers can be put into remission and for how long.
just over 60% of patients saw their tumours shrink or disappear
for around 8% of patients, or one in 12, tumours became undetectable on CT scans
Dr Wungki Park, from Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in the US and who is involved in the trial, said the results were extremely encouraging so far.

"We are beginning to see not only a higher percentage of tumour response rates, but also deeper responses and a near doubling in the duration of disease control, which may eventually translate into longer survival," he said.

Daraxonrasib is a KRAS inhibitor treatment that has already been approved in the US . It works by locking on to and shutting off certain mutations, called RAS , external , found in most pancreatic cancers that drive tumour growth.
Dozens of other cancers, including lung and ovarian, can have similar mutations, meaning the drug might help lots of other patients too.
Dr Godfrey said: "I would hope that the early success that we are beginning to see in pancreatic cancer can also be rolled out to other cancers."
He said longer trials and results were vital. "Cancer can come back and even if scans show there is no sign of it, you don't necessarily know you are cancer-free until more time has passed."

Prof Elena Garralda, chair of a European cancer conference called EORTC where the work is being presented to other doctors, said: "These results are exciting because they show the combined treatment could potentially significantly improve patients' overall survival, as well as the time before tumours start to grow again."
There are 11,500 diagnoses of the disease in Britain each year and around 10,200 deaths, according to Cancer Research UK.
Actor Alan Rickman died of the disease in 2016, five months after diagnosis.
Symptoms can include , external jaundice, itchy skin, darker pee, paler poo, unexplained weight loss, tiredness and high temperature.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crx2: Early efforts to contain coronavirus "were doomed to fail" because the test, trace and isolate system in the UK could only handle a relatively small number of cases, the seventh report of the Covid inquiry says in a damning assessment.
Across 245 pages the inquiry looks at everything from border controls to how well contact tracing worked.
The report said the virus was allowed to spread virtually unchecked in the first few months after community testing and contact tracing was abandoned in mid-March 2020, costing lives.
Ministers said this was because testing capacity was being overwhelmed.
NHS Test and Trace was launched two months later and eventually became one of the biggest testing services in the world per head of population.
In the end, more than £30bn was spent across the UK during the pandemic on testing, tracing and isolating.
But in those early months the four UK nations were "effectively blind" to how quickly Covid was spreading, the inquiry said.

It criticises the government for not having a robust test, trace and isolate system in place to start with, saying this, alongside other failures, meant harsher measures, including lockdown and school closures, were needed.

Inquiry chair Baroness Hallett said the UK should have been better prepared and learnt lessons from other countries that had experience of dealing with outbreaks of other infectious diseases, such as Sars.
Unlike the UK, places such as Hong Kong, South Korea, Singapore and Taiwan had established systems ready to go.
This was despite the fact the UK had run a series of simulation exercises in the years leading up to Covid.
They included Exercise Cygnus into a flu pandemic and Exercise Alice into Mers. Both identified problems relating to test, trace or isolation, which appear not to have been fully acted on.

The report also raises the question of whether the government could have made use of non-government testing facilities in hospitals, universities and the private sector from the start, instead of just relying on 12 government labs.
When people in the UK were told to isolate, "many felt forgotten and let down by the lack of practical or financial support when trying to follow the rules", says the report.
In the early months of the pandemic, estimates suggested less than half of people were complying with the rules around isolating if infected.
Ministers and their advisers discussed this and fines of up to £10,000 were introduced for those who did not comply, which some experts have said was counter-productive.
Changes were made to allow people to claim statutory sick pay.
But it was not until September in England – and later in Scotland and Wales – that £500 financial payments were introduced to help those on low incomes comply.
More also needed to be done to provide practical support for things such as collecting medicines and shopping for food for those who did not have people to call on.

Suspending all flights from China to the UK in February 2020 could "have provided valuable additional time to prepare healthcare systems for the impact of the pandemic", said inquiry chair Baroness Hallett. That didn't happen.
The report says the UK lacked a clear strategy for implementing border control measures early in the pandemic, which left the country in an "extremely vulnerable position".

Although the closure and restriction of borders was noted as "immensely complex", the inquiry said that border control measures could serve as an important tool "to reassure the public and increase confidence."
By April 2020, 93% of countries had put measures in place, such as flight suspensions, border closures and travel restrictions, to control their international borders.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8wy: More than 200 doctors have had their details sent in error to the Times newspaper
The doctors' regulator the General Medical Council (GMC) has apologised after it mistakenly sent information about more than 220 doctors to a national newspaper.
The information included summaries of complaints alleging antisemitism or Islamophobia against the doctors.
For some of the medics involved, it was only when the GMC alerted them to the data breach that they discovered a complaint had been made about them.
The GMC says it is "very sorry" for the incident and has reported itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

The GMC - an independent body that regulates doctors, physician associates and anaesthesia associates to protect patient safety - sent the information about 223 doctors to a journalist at the Times newspaper.
While no names were revealed, GMC identification numbers were included, which would easily allow doctors to be found on the regulator's register.
Some doctors have also raised concerns that their ethnicity was included in the data breach.
All the medics involved have been the subject of a complaint involving either antisemitism or Islamophobia, dating from the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 to September 2026.
The GMC says it has a legal and statutory responsibility to investigate such claims.
Meanwhile, the Times is understood to have promised not to make any of the details public, but has said it will not delete the information.
A spokesman for the doctor's trade union, the British Medical Association (BMA), condemned the release of personal information.

"The BMA is aware that a number of doctors have received communication from the GMC to say that it erroneously sent personal identifiable data about them to the Times newspaper when responding to a media request," it said.
"The GMC must take action to ensure such a breach never occurs again."
The BMA said it would look at ways to support members affected and urged them to make contact via their website.
A doctors' campaign group, The Doctors' Association UK (DAUK), called for an independent investigation into the error.
"If a doctor sent identifiable patient information to a newspaper, they could expect to be referred to the GMC," said Dr Matt Kneale, DAUK co-chairman.

"The GMC should hold itself to the same standard of confidentiality it expects from doctors. It owes every affected doctor a clear account of what it sent, how that happened and what it is doing to get the information deleted."

The doctors' regulator says around a fifth (20%) of the complaints made have already resulted in some sanction related to antisemitism, including two doctors who have been struck off the medical register.
Just over a quarter of complaints over Islamophobia - 26% - have led to disciplinary action.
But other complaints were closed, having failed to reach the threshold for investigation.
The GMC said it had contacted the doctors affected to explain what had happened, to apologise and provide information and support.
A spokesperson added: "We recognise the concern this will cause to both those impacted personally and other registrants and we are very sorry this happened.
"Our priority continues to be supporting those affected and taking steps to reduce the impact of this incident."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6pw: Adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone are allowed but must be rooted in evidence, the regulator said
Five adverts by online healthcare provider Voy have been banned by the watchdog for making misleading claims linked to low testosterone in men.
The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said the adverts promoted Voy's at-home testosterone blood tests in three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads.
It said they were misleading as they linked common symptoms such as irritability and fatigue to low testosterone.
Voy said it had withdrawn the adverts while the investigation was under way and would not run them again.
The NHS says that while testosterone levels in men fall as they age, this is "unlikely" to cause any problems in itself.

It adds , external that while a testosterone deficiency in later life can sometimes be responsible for symptoms such as depression, loss of sex drive, erectile dysfunction, and other physical and emotional symptoms, they are often not linked.
Voy is a company that sells products such as testosterone, menopause and weight loss treatments.
Some of its testosterone test kit adverts drew a backlash online earlier this year when they appeared on the London Underground.
Some described them as "ragebait" for using phrases such as "It's not him, it's his hormones" and "Men get hormonal too".
At the time Voy said it was trying to destigmatise conversations about men's health.
Some of the adverts sparked discussion online after appearing at Tube stations
The ASA's ruling, however, took issue with how some of the adverts "exaggerated the connection between several common symptoms, which can have many possible causes, and low testosterone".
The ASA gave examples such as low sex drive, low energy, loss of motivation and changes in mood.

"While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn't have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation," the watchdog said.
It added that one of the Facebook adverts also included the claim that "low testosterone sneaks up on 1 in 4 men over 30".
The ASA said this was misleading and not supported by the evidence provided by Voy.

Dr Earim Chaudry, chief medical officer for Voy, said: "Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance."

Wednesday's ruling followed two others in August by the watchdog, which found misleading claims in adverts for testosterone testing services from online providers BioID Health and Numan Digital Healthcare.
The rulings form part of a wider ASA investigation into adverts aimed at men concerned about their health.
This has identified a "recurring theme of advertisers playing on insecurities around libido, erectile problems, testosterone and ageing", the regulator said.
The watchdog said adverts for tests and services relating to low testosterone were allowed, but businesses needed to make sure the claims they made were accurate and supported by evidence.

Dr Richard Quinton, who is an expert in testosterone deficiency, said: "It's very easy to get a low testosterone level in any healthy man, simply by doing a blood test in the afternoon, after a meal, when unwell from any cause, or after an all-night sit up."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm0e: From Spring 2027, under 16s will no longer be able to access several social media applications
More than 300,000 young people in Britain will work with researchers to help understand how the UK's forthcoming social media ban for under-16s could affect mental health.
The studies will examine the habits of the children and teenagers, including whether they spend less time on their phones and what they are replacing scrolling with.
Ten different projects have been commissioned, taking place across England, Wales and Scotland, to help reflect a diverse range of teenagers.
The social media ban, beginning in spring 2027, will follow a similar model to that already introduced in Australia to stop children accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.
Apps such as Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, Snapchat and YouTube will be banned under new rules
The work, funded by health charity The Wellcome Trust, will help inform future online safety policies in the UK and internationally, with some early results available before the ban happens.
Researchers will use wearable technology, smartphones, digital diaries and surveys to collect data to see how young people respond to the ban, both physically and mentally.
And they will check whether young people find ways to circumvent restrictions.
Dr Camilla Iannone, research lead at Wellcome, said it was a once-in-a-generation opportunity to study at scale how social media and its restrictions affected youth mental health.
"We really don't think that this is a simple binary question of whether social media is good or bad, or whether restrictions work or don't work.
"Instead, the teams will study whether changing young people's digital environment leads to meaningful changes in their mental health and wellbeing."
Participants are being recruited to reflect a diverse range of young people, including different genders and sexual orientations.
People with existing mental health conditions, such as anxiety and depression, will also be included, as well as young people who are neurodivergent.

Groups have been set up at Cardiff University, the University of Oxford, the University of Birmingham, King's College London, the University of Edinburgh, the University of Manchester, the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, and University College London.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqvg: The government says it will continue a key NHS data contract in England with the controversial US tech giant Palantir until 2029, rather than triggering an early release clause next year.
But ministers are inviting British firms to bid for the contract from 2029, with a procurement programme beginning next summer.

A Commons Committee had called on the government to part ways and appoint a company "more compatible with UK values". Protesters regularly target Palantir over Israel's use of its technology in the Gaza conflict and oppose its use in US immigration enforcement.
The £330m deal, which began in 2024 to help manage hospital waiting lists in England, was due to run until 2031.

The prime minister had faced pressure from some Labour MPs to cut ties with Palantir. They said they were extremely disappointed by the decision, calling the contract "an albatross" hanging around the NHS's neck.
There have also been concerns raised about how patient data will be used .
Palantir, which was co-founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, has interests in US defence and security, and has contracts with the Israeli military.
Health minister James Frith said the move was "not about the politics of executives of suppliers, nor is it about the territories or customers that one company or one supplier makes".
The government says UK companies will be encouraged to tender to avoid overdependence on one supplier.
The timeframe is not fast enough for some members of the government.
Dame Chi Onwurah, Labour MP for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West, said the government needed to "act urgently" to procure "credible domestic alternatives".
"The government should not wait two years, it must start reducing this dependency now," she said.
Former Labour shadow chancellor John McDonnell went further, and accused Palantir of "human rights abuses". He said his constituents in Hayes and Harlington "expect the contract to be ended".
Liberal Democrat health spokeswoman Helen Morgan criticised the company for what she called its "appalling human rights record, run by an ally of Donald Trump".

The British Medical Association, which represents doctors, said it was glad the government had shown it was listening to its concerns about Palantir, but was frustrated the process of changing to another company was further delayed.
Palantir UK said it was right to press forward with the programme which was exceeding targets.

"We are proud of our work to date to help deliver more operations, speed up discharge and reduce the time patients need to wait to find out if they have cancer," Palantir UK senior vice-president Tom Watson said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6m2: Baroness Cass said the current wording of the bill risked "serious unintended consequences"
The author of the independent review into gender identity services for young people says she does not support the current draft bill banning conversion practices - having previously welcomed it.
Baroness Cass told BBC Radio 4's Today programme while it is "desirable" to ban the practices, "the challenge is that we have not yet as far as I can see got a workable bill".

At a parliamentary committee scrutinising the bill, she also said it risked "serious unintended consequences" for parents of children suffering gender distress, or medical professionals working in that area.
They added they would take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as they "want to get this ban right". The government has said the bill would protect LGBT people in England and Wales.
Conversion practices are generally described as interventions, treatments or activities designed to change or suppress someone's sexual orientation or gender identity.
This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.
There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.
When the government introduced its draft legislation , external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it , external .

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not."
She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.
But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".
Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities".
But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.
"Therapeutic interactions can be distressing and often are because you're discussing quite sensitive issues," she told the Today programme.
"So If a young person comes away feeling upset, distressed, angry, that might be the result of a quite appropriate therapeutic intervention but still could be judged as poor professional practice."
She told the committee that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.
"The problem is the chilling effect of professionals knowing that they may be open to complaint, and indeed prosecution," she told the Today programme.
Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but had not had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqjd: Nicola Packer was acquitted of "unlawfully administering to herself a poison or other noxious thing" with the "intent to procure a miscarriage"
Women arrested or convicted for having illegal abortions will have their criminal records wiped as new automatic pardons come into force in England and Wales , external .

Ending the Victorian-era law should avoid traumatic experiences such as that of Nicola Packer, who was recently cleared by a jury after taking medication at home during a Covid lockdown. She had ended a pregnancy without realising she was around 26 weeks pregnant, far beyond the legal 10 week limit.
Her friend Helle Tumbridge told the BBC's Today Programme she had been "treated appallingly" until justice was served.

Labour MP Tonia Antoniazzi, who brought forward the decriminalisation amendment last year, says the change will clear the names of more than 100 women who have been "unnecessarily harmed" by an "outdated" law.
Ms Packer, who was 41 at the time, took pills called mifepristone and misoprostol, which were prescribed over the phone due to Covid restrictions, to end a pregnancy in 2020.
Prosecutors alleged that she knew she had been pregnant for more than 10 weeks, which she denied.
Jurors deliberated for more than six hours to reach their unanimous verdict, clearing her name.
Speaking with the BBC and Nicola's consent, her friend Ms Tumbridge said the whole incident was "incredibly traumatic".
"Nicky had what's known as a cryptic pregnancy - that's when you don't have any sign of a pregnancy, no baby bump, no other symptoms.
"She thought she was just a few weeks pregnant and she sought an abortion and was prescribed that by the NHS. Unfortunately, she was a lot more far gone."
Nicola experienced a stillbirth and went to hospital. The staff there called the police.

"She was arrested. She spent a time in her hospital room recovering with two police officers present, one was a man. She was treated appallingly. She was made to use the toilet with the door open in front of the police officers."
It took five years of investigations for a trial to eventually find her not guilty.
"Of course, by that point the damage had been done," says Tumbridge, "and she'll live with that trauma for the rest of her life."
At the time, The Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists said Nicola's trial demonstrated "just how outdated and harmful" that law was.
It is now no longer a criminal offence for a pregnant woman to terminate her own pregnancy at any stage.
Minister for Victims and Tackling Violence Against Women and Girls, Alex Davies-Jones, said pardoning women for abortion offences related to their own pregnancy had been a priority.
"I'm pleased to be able to commence the change that Parliament voted for.

"For those affected, I know that clear and accessible information about what happens next is vital. Women do not have to take any direct action themselves, but can find out more information online and contact our dedicated casework team."

Heidi Stewart, from the abortion care provider BPAS, said: "While no pardon can undo the distress and trauma these women have experienced, this historic change in the law recognises the profound harm caused by their criminalisation and represents a meaningful step towards justice."

Abortion in England and Wales is legal with an authorised provider up to 24 weeks, with very limited circumstances allowing one after this time, such as when the mother's life is at risk or the child would be born with a severe disability.
It is also legal to take prescribed medication at home if a woman is less than 10 weeks pregnant.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y: The capsule dissolves in the stomach and releases a small sponge which collects cells from the lining of the oesophagus as it's removed
Some people with bad and persistent indigestion should be offered quick "sponge in the gullet" tests to check for oesophageal cancer, new draft guidelines for the NHS in England recommend.
The sponge tests can be carried out in GP surgeries in minutes, and are less invasive than hospital endoscopy checks that instead use a small camera to look inside the body.
The tests are already available in some places but could now be offered across England.
Heartburn or acid reflux can occur with a condition called Barrett's oesophagus that increases the risk of cancer in the long term.

It is thought between one and two adults in every 100 has Barrett's oesophagus, where cells have started to change. Most won't go on to develop cancer, but demand for NHS endoscopy is high, meaning some with the condition aren't checked as often as recommended.
The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) says the sponge tests, already offered in some places, could help give more patients peace of mind.

For the test, patients swallow a small dissolving capsule attached to a thread. Once in the stomach, it releases a tiny sponge. The sponge collect cells from the lining of the gullet as it is gently pulled back out of the patient's mouth by the doctor.

Prof Jonathan Benger, chief executive of NICE, says sponge tests offer a "quick and less invasive" way to detect concerning changes, helping to identify people who should go on to have further tests and treatment.

Prof Peter Johnson, national clinical director for cancer at NHS England, said: "The NHS is always looking for better ways to get to the bottom of people's symptoms, and thousands have already benefited from this incredibly efficient test through pilots we have been running, so it's fantastic it is now being considered for roll out across the country.

"Many people have acid reflux, and having an easier way to check for changes in the lining of the oesophagus can make a big difference for patients, reducing the need for more complicated endoscopy tests and helping the NHS free up resources to find cancers at an earlier stage."
However, no diagnostic test, including endoscopy, identifies every case and people who receive an all-clear sponge test result should still be monitored in the long term, NICE adds.
The sponge tests can help detect oesophageal cancer and Barrett's oesophagus in people with reflux disease.
The oesophagus leads to the stomach. Both are highlighed in red/orange
Reflux can cause heartburn, which is a burning sensation in the middle of your chest, as well as an unpleasant sour taste in your mouth, caused by stomach acid.
A lax or weakened sphincter at the bottom of the oesophagus or food pipe, where it meets the stomach, can be part of the issue, allowing digestive juices to seep up the wrong way.
Being overweight, smoking and drinking alcohol can increase a person's risk of reflux.
